spec.description: Unit circle with twelve labelled coordinate pairs, double-ended coordinate axes, coloured radius families and counterclockwise directed arcs for 30°, 120°, 210° and 300°. Source magenta maps to red and cyan maps to blue. No shaded regions.
spec.mathematics: The point at angle θ is (cos θ,sin θ); tan θ=y/x when x is nonzero. All coordinates and angle endpoints are derived from the unit circle.
spec.answerVisibility: All coordinates, rays and angle annotations are permanent supplied givens. Individual function values occur only in answers.

answer.worked: At $0^\circ$, the point is $(1,0)$. Hence $\sin0^\circ=y=0$.
At $0^\circ$, the point is $(1,0)$. Hence $\cos0^\circ=x=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan0^\circ&=\frac{y}{x}\\&=\frac01\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
At $120^\circ$, the point is $\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Thus $\sin120^\circ=y=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
At $120^\circ$, the point is $\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Thus $\cos120^\circ=x=-\frac12$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan120^\circ&=\frac{y}{x}\\&=\frac{\sqrt3/2}{-1/2}\\&=-\sqrt3\end{aligned}$$
At $300^\circ$, the point is $\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Thus $\sin300^\circ=y=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
At $300^\circ$, the point is $\left(\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Thus $\cos300^\circ=x=\frac12$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan300^\circ&=\frac{y}{x}\\&=\frac{-\sqrt3/2}{1/2}\\&=-\sqrt3\end{aligned}$$
At $210^\circ$, the point is $\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)$. Thus $\cos210^\circ=x=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
At $240^\circ$, the point is $\left(-\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Thus $\sin240^\circ=y=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan150^\circ&=\frac{y}{x}\\&=\frac{1/2}{-\sqrt3/2}\\&=-\frac1{\sqrt3}\end{aligned}$$
At $60^\circ$, the point is $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Thus $\sin60^\circ=y=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
At $30^\circ$, the point is $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$. Thus $\cos30^\circ=x=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan240^\circ&=\frac{y}{x}\\&=\frac{-\sqrt3/2}{-1/2}\\&=\sqrt3\end{aligned}$$
At $150^\circ$, the point is $\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$. Thus $\cos150^\circ=x=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
At $90^\circ$, the point is $(0,1)$. Hence $\cos90^\circ=x=0$.
At $180^\circ$, the point is $(-1,0)$. Hence $\sin180^\circ=y=0$.
At $210^\circ$, the point is $\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)$. Thus $\sin210^\circ=y=-\frac12$.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan330^\circ&=\frac{y}{x}\\&=\frac{-1/2}{\sqrt3/2}\\&=-\frac1{\sqrt3}\end{aligned}$$
At $270^\circ$, the point is $(0,-1)$. Since $\tan\theta=y/x$ and $x=0$, $\tan270^\circ$ is undefined.

answer.worked: Cosine is the horizontal coordinate. The unit circle has $x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ at $30^{\circ}$ and $330^{\circ}$.
Sine is the vertical coordinate. The unit circle has $y=\frac{1}{2}$ at $30^{\circ}$ and $150^{\circ}$.
Sine is the vertical coordinate. The unit circle has $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ at $210^{\circ}$ and $330^{\circ}$.
Sine is the vertical coordinate. The unit circle has $y=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ at $60^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$.
Sine is the vertical coordinate. The unit circle has $y=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ at $240^{\circ}$ and $300^{\circ}$.
Cosine is the horizontal coordinate. The unit circle has $x=\frac{1}{2}$ at $60^{\circ}$ and $300^{\circ}$.
The points with horizontal coordinate $0$ are $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$, giving $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$.
The point with vertical coordinate $-1$ is $(0,-1)$, giving $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
The point with horizontal coordinate $1$ is $(1,0)$, giving $\theta=0^{\circ}$. The angle $360^{\circ}$ is outside the specified interval.

spec.description: Unshaded circle centred at crossing axes, radius labelled 4, and a ray through P at 60 degrees in quadrant I.
spec.mathematics: P=(4 cos 60°,4 sin 60°). The schematic circle radius is not an axis scale.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens and P are visible.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}P&=(4\cos60^{\circ},4\sin60^{\circ})\\&=\left(4\times\frac12,4\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\&=(2,2\sqrt3)\end{aligned}$$

spec.description: Unshaded circle centred at crossing axes, radius labelled 2, and a ray through P at 150 degrees in quadrant II.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens and P are visible.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}P&=(2\cos150^{\circ},2\sin150^{\circ})\\&=(-2\cos30^{\circ},2\sin30^{\circ})\\&=\left(-2\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2},2\times\frac12\right)\\&=(-\sqrt3,1)\end{aligned}$$

spec.description: Unshaded circle centred at crossing axes, radius labelled square root of 2 above the positive horizontal axis, and a ray through P at 315 degrees in quadrant IV.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens and P are visible.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}P&=(\sqrt2\cos315^{\circ},\sqrt2\sin315^{\circ})\\&=(\sqrt2\cos45^{\circ},-\sqrt2\sin45^{\circ})\\&=\left(\sqrt2\times\frac1{\sqrt2},-\sqrt2\times\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\\&=(1,-1)\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt:
The points $P,Q,R,S$ are on the unit circle. $A(1,0)$ and $O$ is the origin. Find the exact coordinates of $P,Q,R,S$ if:

$\angle AOP=60^{\circ}$, $\angle AOQ=120^{\circ}$, $\angle AOR=240^{\circ}$, $\angle AOS=30^{\circ}$.

spec.description: Unit circle with positive axis arrowheads, radii to four marked points, labels P, Q, R, S and A, and numeric labels 1 and −1. The Cartesian-origin O label is omitted under the graph convention.
spec.mathematics: P is at 60°, Q at 120°, R at 240° and S at 330°. S lies 30° clockwise from OA.
spec.answerVisibility: Question figure contains point locations and names, but no coordinate answers.

answer.worked:
On the unit circle, $(x,y)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. The diagram places $S$ in quadrant IV, so its directed angle is $330^{\circ}$.

$\begin{aligned}P&=(\cos60^{\circ},\sin60^{\circ})\\&=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\Q&=(-\cos60^{\circ},\sin60^{\circ})\\&=\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\R&=(-\cos60^{\circ},-\sin60^{\circ})\\&=\left(-\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\S&=(\cos30^{\circ},-\sin30^{\circ})\\&=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)\end{aligned}$

content.prompt: Find the exact value of these trigonometric ratios.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\cos(-60^{\circ})&=\cos300^{\circ}\\&=\cos60^{\circ}\\&=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sin(-120^{\circ})&=\sin240^{\circ}\\&=-\sin60^{\circ}\\&=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\tan(-120^{\circ})&=\tan240^{\circ}\\&=\tan60^{\circ}\\&=\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sin(-315^{\circ})&=\sin45^{\circ}\\&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\tan(-210^{\circ})&=\tan150^{\circ}\\&=-\tan30^{\circ}\\&=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\cos(-225^{\circ})&=\cos135^{\circ}\\&=-\cos45^{\circ}\\&=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\tan420^{\circ}&=\tan60^{\circ}\\&=\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\cos510^{\circ}&=\cos150^{\circ}\\&=-\cos30^{\circ}\\&=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sin495^{\circ}&=\sin135^{\circ}\\&=\sin45^{\circ}\\&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\sin690^{\circ}&=\sin330^{\circ}\\&=-\sin30^{\circ}\\&=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Prove, using exact values, that:

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=-\sin30^\circ(-\cos30^\circ)-\cos30^\circ\sin30^\circ\\&=\sin30^\circ\cos30^\circ-\cos30^\circ\sin30^\circ\\&=\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac12\\&=0=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=\sin60^\circ\cos45^\circ+\cos60^\circ\sin45^\circ\\&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)+\frac12\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\\&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}+\frac1{2\sqrt2}\\&=\frac{\sqrt3+1}{2\sqrt2}=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=\frac{\sin45^\circ-(-\cos60^\circ)}{\sin45^\circ+(-\cos60^\circ)}\\&=\frac{\frac1{\sqrt2}+\frac12}{\frac1{\sqrt2}-\frac12}\\&=\frac{\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}}{\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}}\\&=\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2-\sqrt2}\times\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2+\sqrt2}\\&=\frac{4+4\sqrt2+2}{4-2}\\&=\frac{6+4\sqrt2}{2}\\&=3+2\sqrt2=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=(\sin30^\circ+0+(-\tan45^\circ))^2\\&=\left(\frac12-1\right)^2\\&=\frac14.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{RHS}&=(\sin45^\circ)^2(-\cos45^\circ)^2\\&=\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^2\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^2\\&=\frac14.\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\mathrm{LHS}=\mathrm{RHS}$.

$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{LHS}&=\frac{\sin60^\circ}{-\tan60^\circ}-\frac{-\cos60^\circ}{\left(\frac1{-\tan45^\circ}\right)}\\&=\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)}{-\sqrt3}-\frac{\left(-\frac12\right)}{-1}\\&=-\frac12-\frac12\\&=-1.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{RHS}&=\tan^2 60^\circ-\frac1{\sin^2 30^\circ}\\&=(\sqrt3)^2-\frac1{\left(\frac12\right)^2}\\&=3-\frac1{\left(\frac14\right)}\\&=3-4\\&=-1.\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\mathrm{LHS}=\mathrm{RHS}$.

answer.worked: The sine graph passes through $(0^{\circ},0)$, so $\sin 0^{\circ}=0$.
At $180^{\circ}$, the cosine graph has height $-1$, so $\cos 180^{\circ}=-1$.
The cosine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $90^{\circ}$, so $\cos 90^{\circ}=0$.
The tangent graph passes through $(0^{\circ},0)$, so $\tan 0^{\circ}=0$.
At $90^{\circ}$, the sine graph has height $1$, so $\sin 90^{\circ}=1$.
At $0^{\circ}$, the cosine graph has height $1$, so $\cos 0^{\circ}=1$.
At $270^{\circ}$, the sine graph has height $-1$, so $\sin 270^{\circ}=-1$.
The cosine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $270^{\circ}$, so $\cos 270^{\circ}=0$.
The sine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $180^{\circ}$, so $\sin 180^{\circ}=0$.
The tangent graph has no point at $270^{\circ}$; its branches approach a vertical asymptote there. Thus $\tan 270^{\circ}$ is undefined.
The tangent graph has no point at $90^{\circ}$; its branches approach a vertical asymptote there. Thus $\tan 90^{\circ}$ is undefined.
The tangent graph crosses the horizontal axis at $180^{\circ}$, so $\tan 180^{\circ}=0$.

content.prompt:
Consider the graphs of $y=\cos x$ and $y=\sin x$ on the same axis.

Decide whether the following statements are true or false.

spec.description: Two black labelled curves on common rectangular axes and a fine grey grid. The graph extends beyond the plotted domain to provide the source margins. Increased width preserves readable labels and the fine grid.
spec.mathematics: y=sin x and y=cos x for 0<=x<=360 degrees. Minor grid steps 10 degrees and 0.1; major grid steps 45 degrees and 0.5. Labelled horizontal values 0, 90, 180, 270, 360 degrees; labelled vertical values -1 and 1.
spec.answerVisibility: Both curves, their labels, axes and grid remain visible in student and answer editions.

answer.worked: On the sine graph, the ordinate at $60^{\circ}$ is positive and the ordinate at $200^{\circ}$ is negative. Hence $\sin60^{\circ}>\sin200^{\circ}$.
The sine graph is above the axis at $100^{\circ}$ and below it at $300^{\circ}$. Thus $\sin100^{\circ}>\sin300^{\circ}$.
On the sine graph, the ordinate at $135^{\circ}$ is higher than the ordinate at $10^{\circ}$. Thus $\sin135^{\circ}>\sin10^{\circ}$.
The sine graph has the same ordinate at $200^{\circ}$ and $340^{\circ}$, so $\sin200^{\circ}=\sin340^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph is positive at $70^{\circ}$ and negative at $125^{\circ}$. Thus $\cos70^{\circ}>\cos125^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph is positive at $315^{\circ}$ and negative at $135^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos315^{\circ}>\cos135^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph has the same ordinate at $310^{\circ}$ and $50^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos310^{\circ}=\cos50^{\circ}$.
Both ordinates are negative, but the cosine graph at $95^{\circ}$ is closer to zero and higher than at $260^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos95^{\circ}>\cos260^{\circ}$.
The sine graph at $90^{\circ}$ and the cosine graph at $360^{\circ}$ both have ordinate $1$.
At $180^{\circ}$, the cosine graph has ordinate $-1$ and the sine graph has ordinate $0$. These values are unequal.
The sine graph at $210^{\circ}$ has ordinate $-0.5$, which is higher than its ordinate near $-1$ at $285^{\circ}$. Hence $\sin210^{\circ}>\sin285^{\circ}$.
The cosine graph is positive at $15^{\circ}$ and negative at $115^{\circ}$. Hence $\cos15^{\circ}>\cos115^{\circ}$.

content.prompt: $f(x)=\sin x+\cos(90^{\circ}-x)$. Decide whether $f(x)$ is odd, even, or neither.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\sin x+\sin x\\f(x)&=2\sin x\\f(-x)&=2\sin(-x)\\f(-x)&=-2\sin x\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $f$ is odd.

content.prompt: $f(x)=x^2\sin(-x)+x\cos(-x)$. Decide whether $f(x)$ is odd, even, or neither.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=-x^2\sin x+x\cos x\\f(-x)&=-(-x)^2\sin(-x)+(-x)\cos(-x)\\f(-x)&=x^2\sin x-x\cos x\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $f$ is odd.

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$. Remember, to solve quadratic equations we need to factorise.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\cos\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\\\cos\theta&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\cos\theta=\frac12.\end{align*}$$
For $\cos\theta=0$, $\theta=90^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.
For $\cos\theta=\frac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\frac12)=60^{\circ}$. Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=60^{\circ},90^{\circ},270^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(\sin\theta+1)&=0\\\sin\theta&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\sin\theta=-1.\end{align*}$$
For $\sin\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
For $\sin\theta=-1$, $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}\tan^2\theta-\tan\theta&=0\\\tan\theta(\tan\theta-1)&=0\\\tan\theta&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\tan\theta=1.\end{align*}$$
For $\tan\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
For $\tan\theta=1$, $A=\tan^{-1}(1)=45^{\circ}$. Tangent is positive in Q1 and Q3, so $\theta=45^{\circ},225^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=0^{\circ},45^{\circ},180^{\circ},225^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-1&=0\\(\sqrt2\cos\theta-1)(\sqrt2\cos\theta+1)&=0\\\cos\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt2}\quad\text{or}\quad\cos\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.\end{align*}$$
$A=\cos^{-1}(\frac1{\sqrt2})=45^{\circ}$. The positive and negative ratios give solutions in all four quadrants.
$\theta=45^{\circ},135^{\circ},225^{\circ},315^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}3\tan^2\theta-1&=0\\(\sqrt3\tan\theta-1)(\sqrt3\tan\theta+1)&=0\\\tan\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt3}\quad\text{or}\quad\tan\theta=-\frac1{\sqrt3}.\end{align*}$$
$A=\tan^{-1}(\frac1{\sqrt3})=30^{\circ}$. The positive and negative ratios give solutions in all four quadrants.
$\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ},210^{\circ},330^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta-1&=0\quad\text{or}\quad\sin\theta+1=0\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad\sin\theta=-1.\end{align*}$$
For $\sin\theta=\frac12$, $A=\sin^{-1}(\frac12)=30^{\circ}$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ}$.
For $\sin\theta=-1$, $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.

content.prompt: Jimmy solved $\tan^2\theta=\tan\theta$ for $\theta\in[0^\circ,360^\circ)$ by dividing both sides by $\tan\theta$ first. He got the solutions $45^\circ$ and $225^\circ$, which are not all the solutions.

answer.short: Dividing by $\tan\theta$ assumes $\tan\theta\ne0$, losing $\theta=0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. Move all terms to the left, factorise and use the null factor law.
answer.worked:
Dividing by $\tan\theta$ excludes the case $\tan\theta=0$. Instead,
$$\begin{align*}\tan^2\theta-\tan\theta&=0\\\tan\theta(\tan\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\tan\theta=0$ or $\tan\theta=1$.

For $\tan\theta=0$, $\theta=0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$.

For $\tan\theta=1$, the reference angle is $45^\circ$ and tangent is positive in Q1 and Q3, giving $\theta=45^\circ$ or $225^\circ$.

All solutions are $0^\circ,45^\circ,180^\circ,225^\circ$; Jimmy missed $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^\circ,360^\circ)$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin^2\theta-3\sin\theta+1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=1$.

For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$, $A=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac12)=30^\circ$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=30^\circ$ or $180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ$.

For $\sin\theta=1$, $\theta=90^\circ$.

Thus $\theta=30^\circ,90^\circ,150^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-3&=0\\(2\cos\theta-3)(\cos\theta+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=\tfrac32$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

Since $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$, $\cos\theta=\tfrac32$ has no solution.

For $\cos\theta=-1$, $\theta=180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\cos\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=0$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.

For $\cos\theta=0$, $\theta=90^\circ$ or $270^\circ$.

For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac12)=60^\circ$. Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=60^\circ$ or $360^\circ-60^\circ=300^\circ$.

Thus $\theta=60^\circ,90^\circ,270^\circ,300^\circ$.

The denominators require $\cos\theta\ne0$. Multiplying by $\cos^2\theta$ gives
$$\begin{align*}1+\cos\theta-2\cos^2\theta&=0\\2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1&=0\\(2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$ or $\cos\theta=1$.

For $\cos\theta=-\tfrac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac12)=60^\circ$. Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3, giving $\theta=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$ or $180^\circ+60^\circ=240^\circ$.

For $\cos\theta=1$, $\theta=0^\circ$ in the stated domain. The endpoint $360^\circ$ is excluded.

Thus $\theta=0^\circ,120^\circ,240^\circ$.

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$. Answer to the nearest minute where necessary.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=0$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.
For $\sin\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, the reference angle is $60^{\circ}$ and cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, giving $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=0^{\circ},60^{\circ},180^{\circ},300^{\circ}$. The upper endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.

$$\begin{align*}2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=-1$.
For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$, the reference angle is $30^{\circ}$ and sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, giving $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ}$.
For $\sin\theta=-1$, $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.

Since the denominators require $\cos\theta\ne0$, multiply by $\cos^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}1+2\cos\theta&=8\cos^2\theta\\8\cos^2\theta-2\cos\theta-1&=0\\(4\cos\theta+1)(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\cos\theta=-\tfrac14$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.
For $\cos\theta=-\tfrac14$, use the positive ratio:
$$A=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac14\right).$$
Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3, so $\theta=180^{\circ}-A,180^{\circ}+A$, giving $104^{\circ}29',255^{\circ}31'$ to the nearest minute.
For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=60^{\circ},104^{\circ}29',255^{\circ}31',300^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}3\cos^2\theta+5\cos\theta-2&=0\\(3\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\cos\theta=\tfrac13$ or $\cos\theta=-2$. Reject $-2$ because $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$.
$$A=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac13\right).$$
Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=A,360^{\circ}-A$.
To the nearest minute, $\theta=70^{\circ}32',289^{\circ}28'$.

Since the denominators require $\sin\theta\ne0$, multiply by $\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}4-4\sin\theta-15\sin^2\theta&=0\\15\sin^2\theta+4\sin\theta-4&=0\\(5\sin\theta-2)(3\sin\theta+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=\tfrac25$ or $\sin\theta=-\tfrac23$.
For $\sin\theta=\tfrac25$, let $A=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac25)$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=A,180^{\circ}-A$, giving $23^{\circ}35',156^{\circ}25'$.
For $\sin\theta=-\tfrac23$, let $B=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac23)$. Sine is negative in Q3 and Q4, so $\theta=180^{\circ}+B,360^{\circ}-B$, giving $221^{\circ}49',318^{\circ}11'$.
All angles are rounded to the nearest minute.

$$\begin{align*}4\sin^3\theta-3\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(4\sin^2\theta-3)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=0$ or $\sin^2\theta=\tfrac34$.
For $\sin\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
Otherwise $\sin\theta=\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, with reference angle $60^{\circ}$. Positive sine gives $60^{\circ},120^{\circ}$; negative sine gives $240^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=0^{\circ},60^{\circ},120^{\circ},180^{\circ},240^{\circ},300^{\circ}$. The upper endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.

content.prompt: Solve $2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1=0$ for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$.

answer.worked:
Factorise using PSF: the product is $-2$, the sum is $-1$, and the factors are $-2$ and $1$.
$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos^2\theta-2\cos\theta+\cos\theta-1&=0\\2\cos\theta(\cos\theta-1)+(\cos\theta-1)&=0\\(2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-1)&=0\\\cos\theta=-\frac12\quad\text{or}&\quad\cos\theta=1.\end{align*}$$
For $\cos\theta=-\frac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\frac12)=60^{\circ}$. Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3, so $\theta=120^{\circ},240^{\circ}$.
For $\cos\theta=1$, $\theta=0^{\circ}$.
Hence $\theta=0^{\circ},120^{\circ},240^{\circ}$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find, correct to the nearest degree, the angles of inclination of the two lines.

answer.worked:
For $5y=9x$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac95x\\m_1&=\frac95\\\theta_1&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac95\right)\\\theta_1&\approx61^\circ.\end{align*}$$
For $5y+9x=45$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=-\frac95x+9\\m_2&=-\frac95\\\theta_2&=\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac95\right)+180^\circ\\\theta_2&\approx119^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What sort of triangle has been formed?

answer.worked: The base angles are $\theta_1$ and $180^\circ-\theta_2$. Since the gradients have equal magnitudes and opposite signs, $\theta_2=180^\circ-\theta_1$. Thus the two base angles are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.

answer.worked:
For $y=\sqrt3x$: $\tan\theta_1=\sqrt3$, so $\theta_1=60^\circ$.
For $y=-\sqrt3x+6\sqrt3$: $\tan\theta_2=-\sqrt3$, so $\theta_2=\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt3)+180^\circ=120^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Angle at the origin}&=60^\circ\\\text{Angle at the }x\text{-intercept}&=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ\\\text{Third angle}&=180^\circ-60^\circ-60^\circ=60^\circ\end{align*}$$

For $y=2x$: $\tan\theta_1=2$, so $\theta_1=\tan^{-1}(2)\approx63^\circ$.
For $x+y=9$: $y=-x+9$, so $\tan\theta_2=-1$ and $\theta_2=\tan^{-1}(-1)+180^\circ=135^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Angle at the origin}&\approx63^\circ\\\text{Angle at the }x\text{-intercept}&=180^\circ-135^\circ=45^\circ\\\text{Third angle}&\approx180^\circ-63^\circ-45^\circ=72^\circ\end{align*}$$

Parts a to d are signposted routine procedures: gradient, inclination angle, point-gradient equation, midpoint, and a product-of-gradients perpendicularity check. Part e needs interpretation, since BD is the perpendicular bisector of AC and so BA = BC. Part f needs the student to see that BD is the height, which is a small reframing. Part g is the hardest essential demand and is unsignposted. The student must reframe the rhombus as ABCE with diagonals AC and BE bisecting each other at D, then reflect B through D to get E. children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the gradient of line $AC$ and hence determine $\theta$, correct to the nearest degree.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}m_{AC}&=\frac{4-0}{7-1}\\m_{AC}&=\frac23\\\tan\theta&=\frac23\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac23\right)\\\theta&\approx34^\circ.\end{align*}$$

Using $A(1,0)$ and $m_{AC}=\frac23$:
$$\begin{align*}y-0&=\frac23(x-1)\\3y&=2x-2\\2x-3y-2&=0.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the coordinates of the midpoint $D$ of $AC$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}D&=\left(\frac{1+7}{2},\frac{0+4}{2}\right)\\D&=(4,2).\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}m_{BD}&=\frac{2-8}{4-0}\\m_{BD}&=-\frac32\\m_{AC}m_{BD}&=\frac23\left(-\frac32\right)\\m_{AC}m_{BD}&=-1.\end{align*}$$
The gradients have product $-1$, so $AC\perp BD$.
$BD$ is perpendicular to $AC$ and passes through its midpoint, so $BD$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AC$. Therefore $BA=BC$, and triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Find the area of this triangle.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}AC&=\sqrt{(7-1)^2+(4-0)^2}\\AC&=\sqrt{52}\\BD&=\sqrt{(4-0)^2+(2-8)^2}\\BD&=\sqrt{52}.\end{align*}$$
Since $BD\perp AC$, $BD$ is the perpendicular height.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=\frac12\times AC\times BD\\\text{Area}&=\frac12\times\sqrt{52}\times\sqrt{52}\\\text{Area}&=26\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: g
children.prompt: Write the coordinates of a point $E$ such that $ABCE$ is a rhombus.

answer.worked:
The diagonals $AC$ and $BE$ must bisect each other at $D(4,2)$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{0+x_E}{2}&=4\\x_E&=8\\\frac{8+y_E}{2}&=2\\y_E&=-4.\end{align*}$$
Thus $E=(8,-4)$. The diagonals bisect each other and are perpendicular, so $ABCE$ is a rhombus.

content.prompt:
Two triangles are shown, with sides 6 cm and 4 cm. The angle opposite the 4 cm side is $36^\circ$.

Find, in each case, the angle opposite the 6 cm side, correct to the nearest degree.

spec.description: Two triangles side by side with horizontal bases and 36° at their lower-right vertices. The left triangle has an obtuse lower-left angle; the right has an acute lower-left angle. Ordinary source strokes are rendered black.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the angle opposite the 6 cm side.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\theta}{6}&=\frac{\sin36^\circ}{4}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{6\sin36^\circ}{4}.\end{align*}$$
The acute possibility is
$$\begin{align*}\theta_1&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{6\sin36^\circ}{4}\right)\\\theta_1&\approx61.8454^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The obtuse possibility is
$$\begin{align*}\theta_2&=180^\circ-\theta_1\\\theta_2&\approx118.1546^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Both are valid because $36^\circ+118.1546^\circ<180^\circ$.

The left triangle has the obtuse angle, so its required angle is $118^\circ$. The right triangle has the acute angle, so its required angle is $62^\circ$, to the nearest degree.

content.prompt:
The equation $2x+3y+4=0$ makes an angle with the positive $x$-axis.
Which of the following is closest to the size of the angle?
A. $34^\circ$
B. $56^\circ$
C. $124^\circ$
D. $146^\circ$

answer.worked:
First, rearrange the equation of the line into gradient-intercept form ($y = mx + c$) to determine its gradient $m$:
$$\begin{align*}
2x + 3y + 4 &= 0 \\
3y &= -2x - 4 \\
y &= -\frac{2}{3}x - \frac{4}{3}
\end{align*}$$
The gradient of the line is $m = -\frac{2}{3}$. The relationship between the gradient and the angle $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis is $m = \tan\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}
\tan\theta &= -\frac{2}{3} \\
\theta &= 180^\circ+\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) \\
&\approx 146.31^\circ
\end{align*}$$
Therefore, the closest angle is $146^\circ$.
Correct answer: D.

content.prompt:
Find all the values of $\theta$, where $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 360^\circ$ such that
$\sin(\theta - 60^\circ) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

answer.worked:
Given the domain $0^\circ \leq \theta \leq 360^\circ$, the domain for $(\theta - 60^\circ)$ is:
$$-60^\circ \leq \theta - 60^\circ \leq 300^\circ$$
The related acute angle for $\sin \alpha = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is $60^\circ$.
Since sine is negative, the angle must lie in the third or fourth quadrants (or a negative angle in the fourth quadrant).
Within the adjusted domain $[-60^\circ, 300^\circ]$, the possible values for $(\theta - 60^\circ)$ are:
$$\theta - 60^\circ = -60^\circ \text{ (4th quadrant negative angle)}$$
$$\theta - 60^\circ = 180^\circ + 60^\circ = 240^\circ \text{ (3rd quadrant)}$$
$$\theta - 60^\circ = 360^\circ - 60^\circ = 300^\circ \text{ (4th quadrant positive angle)}$$
Solving for $\theta$ in each case:
$$\begin{align*}
\theta &= -60^\circ + 60^\circ = 0^\circ \\
\theta &= 240^\circ + 60^\circ = 300^\circ \\
\theta &= 300^\circ + 60^\circ = 360^\circ
\end{align*}$$
So the values are $\theta = 0^\circ, 300^\circ, 360^\circ$.

content.prompt:
Which of the following statements is correct?
$$\text{A. }\forall a,b\in\mathbb{R},\quad \sin a<\sin b\Rightarrow a<b$$
$$\text{B. }\forall a,b\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right],\quad \sin a<\sin b\Rightarrow a<b$$
$$\text{C. }\forall a,b\in\mathbb{R},\quad \cos a<\cos b\Rightarrow a<b$$
$$\text{D. }\forall a,b\in[0,\pi],\quad \cos a<\cos b\Rightarrow a<b$$

answer.short: B. Sine is strictly increasing on the given interval.
answer.worked:
The sine function is strictly increasing on $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so $\sin a<\sin b$ implies $a<b$ on this interval.
Sine is not increasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$, and cosine is decreasing on $[0,\pi]$.
Correct answer: B.

content.prompt: Find all possible lengths of the third side of triangle $ABC$ given $AB=6.2\text{ cm}$, $\angle ABC=35^\circ$ and $AC=4.1\text{ cm}$. Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
By the sine rule,
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{\sin C}{6.2}&=\frac{\sin35^\circ}{4.1}\\\sin C&=\frac{6.2\sin35^\circ}{4.1}.\end{aligned}$$
Let $\alpha=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{6.2\sin35^\circ}{4.1}\right)$. Then $C=\alpha$ or $180^\circ-\alpha$. Both are valid because $35^\circ+C<180^\circ$ in each case.

For $C=\alpha$,
$$\begin{aligned}A&=180^\circ-35^\circ-\alpha\\BC&=\frac{4.1\sin(145^\circ-\alpha)}{\sin35^\circ}\\BC&\approx7.1\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}$$
For $C=180^\circ-\alpha$,
$$\begin{aligned}A&=180^\circ-35^\circ-(180^\circ-\alpha)\\A&=\alpha-35^\circ\\BC&=\frac{4.1\sin(\alpha-35^\circ)}{\sin35^\circ}\\BC&\approx3.0\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}$$
The third side is $7.1\text{ cm}$ or $3.0\text{ cm}$, to 1 decimal place.

content.prompt: Find the exact value of the area of $\triangle KLM$ and hence find the exact value of $x$.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle KLM with horizontal base LM. N lies between K and M, and LN divides the angle at L into two labelled 30-degree angles. Ordinary lines and labels use black.
spec.mathematics: KL=3, LM=6, angle KLN=30 degrees, angle NLM=30 degrees, LN=x. Coordinates are derived from these relationships; no coordinate values or additional measurements are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: All edges, names, angle labels and supplied lengths are permanent question givens. The numerical value of x is absent.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}
\angle KLM&=30^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\\
&=60^{\circ}\\
\operatorname{Area}(\triangle KLM)&=\frac12(3)(6)\sin60^{\circ}\\
&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}.
\end{aligned}$$
Since $N$ lies on $KM$, the two smaller triangle areas add to the whole triangle area.
$$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Area}(\triangle KLN)+\operatorname{Area}(\triangle NLM)&=\operatorname{Area}(\triangle KLM)\\
\frac12(3)x\sin30^{\circ}+\frac12(6)x\sin30^{\circ}&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\\
\frac34x+\frac32x&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\\
\frac{9x}{4}&=\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\\
x&=2\sqrt3.
\end{aligned}$$

content.prompt: Solve $4\cos^2\theta+2\sin\theta=3$ for $0\leq\theta<360^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Using $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}4(1-\sin^2\theta)+2\sin\theta&=3\\4-4\sin^2\theta+2\sin\theta&=3\\4\sin^2\theta-2\sin\theta-1&=0\\\sin\theta&=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{(-2)^2-4(4)(-1)}}{8}\\\sin\theta&=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{4}\end{align*}$$
For $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4}>0$, use quadrants 1 and 2:
$$\begin{align*}A&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4}\right)\\A&=54^\circ\\\theta&=54^\circ\text{ or }180^\circ-54^\circ\\\theta&=54^\circ\text{ or }126^\circ\end{align*}$$
For $\sin\theta=\dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{4}<0$, use the positive ratio for the reference angle and quadrants 3 and 4:
$$\begin{align*}A&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\right)\\A&=18^\circ\\\theta&=180^\circ+18^\circ\text{ or }360^\circ-18^\circ\\\theta&=198^\circ\text{ or }342^\circ\end{align*}$$
To the nearest degree, $\theta=54^\circ,126^\circ,198^\circ,342^\circ$.

Worked example: Solve $2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1=0$ for $0\le\theta<360^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1&=0\\(2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1)&=0\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $A=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac12)=60^{\circ}$. Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=60^{\circ}$ or $360^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=300^{\circ}$.

For $\cos\theta=-1$, $\theta=180^{\circ}$.

Thus $\theta=60^{\circ},180^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.

Key ideas: 1. Because $\sin\theta=\sin($[[$180^\circ-\theta$]]$)$, the sine rule can give an acute and an obtuse angle. This is the [[ambiguous case]]. 2. For an acute angle $A$, if $a<b\sin A$ then [[no]] triangle exists, and if $b\sin A<a<b$ then [[two]] triangles exist. 3. Reject the obtuse angle $\theta'$ if $\theta'$ plus the given angle is [[$\ge180^\circ$]].

entries.description: Investigation Sign of trigonometric ratios in Q2

In Q2, the point P has a negative x-coordinate and a positive y-coordinate.
Since cos θ = x-coordinate, and x is negative in Q2, cos θ is negative.
Since sin θ = y-coordinate, and y is positive in Q2, sin θ is positive.
Since tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = positive / negative, tan θ is negative.

3. Rewrite trig ratio with acute reference angle and the correct sign.

entries.description:
If the question doesn’t tell you whether a triangle has an acute or obtuse angle:
1. Use sine rule to find the unknown acute angle θ.
2. Find the obtuse angle θ′ = 180° − θ.
3. Add θ′ to the given angle. If the sum > 180°, it is not a valid possibility (angle sum of triangle cannot exceed 180°).
Warning: Diagrams are never drawn to scale. In an exam, if you see a sine rule question worth 3 marks or more, it is likely the ambiguous case and marks will be awarded for justifying all possible answers.
